task: 1.1 — Resolve shared build tools and config by package ownership
status: GREEN -- all Task 1.1 acceptance items are satisfied, including real headless-browser execution. Implementation, fixtures, and real Node-suite consumer regressions were GREEN as of reviewerFeedbackRound3. The one remaining item -- real headless-browser execution of the WebdriverIO suites -- was blocked purely by a local machine gap (the automatic chromedriver-for-testing installer 404ing for the exact installed Chrome patch version, with only empty/failed-download cache entries present); it is now closed by manually provisioning the real chromedriver binary into the same local cache path WDIO expects (a one-time, local-machine-only fix, no repository or CI file touched -- see finalBrowserSuiteEvidence). All five browser-runner suites (bitcore-lib, bitcore-lib-cash, bitcore-lib-doge, bitcore-lib-ltc, bitcore-mnemonic) now pass their full Node+real-headless-Chrome pipeline with exit 0. Across this review, an external reviewer's passes identified and I fixed: ambient-PATH reliance for nyc/mocha, fixture symlinks that would dangle once dependencies hoist (twice -- a second instance was introduced and then fixed in the space-path fixture), missing test-bundle-generation/discovery coverage, and a stub-vs-real-Browserify accuracy gap in the space-path fixture -- see reviewerFeedback, reviewerFeedbackRound2, and reviewerFeedbackRound3 below.

redEvidence.diagnosedRootCause: packages/bitcore-build/index.js resolves Browserify/Karma/WebdriverIO/Istanbul/Mocha binaries and its own karma.conf.js/wdio.conf.js by concatenating fixed-depth, process.cwd()-relative strings ('./node_modules/@bitpay-labs/bitcore-build/node_modules/.bin/<tool>', falling back to './node_modules/.bin/<tool>'), rather than resolving from the owning package's own location (e.g. __dirname or the module's resolved manifest/bin metadata). This physical-path assumption matches only Lerna's current per-package bootstrap layout, where each consumer gets its own nested 'node_modules/@bitpay-labs/bitcore-build' symlink pointing at a copy of bitcore-build that has its own nested 'node_modules/.bin' with its dependencies. Under npm workspaces, bitcore-build is linked once at the repository root and its dependencies hoist there too, so neither hardcoded depth exists under any consumer directory, even though the tool and the workspace are genuinely installed.

Node's module resolution realpaths through symlinks for cache identity, so the copied helper's own 'require("gulp-shell")' resolves to the same real, cached module object as the test's, letting the test capture the exact command constructed without altering the helper's logic. The unmodified helper content is exercised for real: startGulp('lib', {}) followed by invoking the returned 'browser:uncompressed' gulp-shell task.

implementation.summary: packages/bitcore-build/index.js no longer guesses fixed-depth, cwd-relative paths for any tool it invokes (browserify, karma, @wdio's wdio binary, nyc, mocha) or for its own karma.conf.js/wdio.conf.js. Every tool is resolved from bitcore-build's own location (__dirname) via that dependency's real package manifest/bin metadata (resolvePackageDir()/resolveBin()), and its own shared browser configs resolve via path.join(__dirname, ...) instead of a consumer-cwd guess about where bitcore-build physically lives. Resolved paths are shell-quoted (quote()) so checkout locations containing spaces still work.

files.change: Removed the buildPath/buildBinPath fixed-depth string construction and the six fs.existsSync fallback probes (browserify/karma/wdio/istanbul/plato/mocha paths -- istanbulPath, platoPath, and mochaPath were dead: istanbul and plato are unused (plato's own task is already commented out) and test:node never referenced mochaPath, relying instead on ambient PATH -- removing them is not a fallback substitution, it is deleting code that did nothing). Added resolvePackageDir() (locates an installed package's real root directory from its normal require.resolve()'d entry point, walking up to the nearest package.json whose own "name" matches -- needed because @wdio/cli declares a strict "exports" map that rejects a direct require.resolve('@wdio/cli/package.json') subpath, discovered by running the fixture against the real dependency rather than a hand-rolled stub) and resolveBin() (reads that package's own 'bin' manifest field to get the real script path) and quote() (shell-quotes a path for spaces). karma.conf.js/wdio.conf.js default paths now resolve via path.join(__dirname, ...). test:node's 'nyc mocha -- --recursive' (originally a bare command name, relying on ambient PATH -- see reviewerFeedback) now uses resolveBin('nyc')/resolveBin('mocha') the same way as the browser tools. resolvePackageDir is also exported as a property of the module (module.exports.resolvePackageDir) so focused tests can reuse the same real dependency-location logic instead of duplicating or hardcoding it.

files: ['../../../tests.js'] (relative to karma.conf.js's own on-disk location, which only lined up under Lerna's fixed per-package nesting depth) replaced with files: [path.join(process.cwd(), 'tests.js')] -- the same consumer-cwd resolution wdio.conf.js already used correctly. Verified by loading the module with a fake config recorder against a real, on-disk generated tests.js (see greenEvidence).

Replaced the unusable "test": "gulp test" script (bitcore-build has no own gulpfile) with "test": "node --test test/*.test.cjs", matching the project's existing test/workspaces/*.test.cjs convention. Added "mocha": "^11.7.5" and "nyc": "^18.0.0" as declared dependencies: test:node's shell command ('nyc mocha -- --recursive') invoked both undeclared, resolving only via inherited PATH from whichever ancestor node_modules/.bin happened to provide them (currently the root's devDependencies) -- ownership is now explicit at the package that actually runs them, and (after reviewerFeedback) the invocation itself resolves them the same way as every other tool.

Regenerated via `npm install` inside packages/bitcore-build after the manifest change (still that package's own independently tracked lock at this pre-cutover stage; Task 2.1 removes all 18 backend child locks). Verified every other top-level declared dependency's resolved version is unchanged (browserify 16.5.0, karma 6.4.0, @wdio/cli 9.12.1, webdriverio 9.12.1, gulp 4.0.2, gulp-shell 0.6.5, gulp-rename 1.4.0, gulp-terser 1.2.0, chai 4.2.0, lodash 4.17.15, brfs 2.0.2, karma-chrome-launcher 3.1.1, karma-mocha 2.0.1) -- the large lock diff (added 223 packages, removed 33, changed 38) is nyc/mocha's own substantial transitive tree, not a resolution regression elsewhere. gulp-mocha's own pre-existing nested mocha@6.2.3 (a different, older transitive instance) is untouched.

reviewerFeedback.source: External agentic reviewer pass on the first GREEN submission.
reviewerFeedback.verdict: Three of four points were valid and are fixed; the fourth (browser-execution wording) was a legitimate objection to how the result was phrased, also fixed. No point was rejected outright, though point 1's severity for this repository's actual invocation pattern is narrower than the review implied -- see below.

points.claim: Node tool resolution still depends on ambient PATH: test:node invokes 'nyc mocha' by bare name; gulp-shell only adds the consumer's node_modules/.bin to PATH, so a nested/hoisted installation could fail or silently run a different version.
points.disposition: Fixed, and partially disputed on severity. Fixed: test:node now resolves nyc/mocha via resolveBin(), identical to the other tools -- see implementation above and greenEvidence's captured-command output. Disputed: the claim that this would concretely fail under a hoisted installation is not correct for how this repository actually invokes these scripts. Verified empirically (not merely reasoned): a plain nested npm package (package.json only, no 'workspaces' field) with a tool present ONLY at the root's node_modules/.bin, and a child script that spawns that tool by bare name via `child_process.spawn(name, {shell:true, env:{...process.env}})` (the same double-spawn shape gulp-shell uses under the hood) invoked via `npm run <script>` from the child directory, successfully found and ran the root-only tool. This is because npm's own script runner (not gulp-shell) walks every ancestor directory's node_modules/.bin when constructing PATH before spawning the script (the same general npm behavior Node's own module resolution uses, unrelated to workspaces specifically), and that already-augmented PATH is what gulp-shell's spawn inherits before prepending the consumer's own .bin on top of it. Every root test:<package> alias in this repository (and, per the plan's design, every future workspace-scoped equivalent) is invoked through `npm run`, so the concrete 'nested installation fails' scenario the review describes does not reproduce in this repository's actual invocation path. The fix was made anyway because resolving by ownership (a) removes reliance on that npm behavior entirely, (b) eliminates any possibility of an unrelated, earlier-on-PATH nyc/mocha silently shadowing the declared ones, and (c) makes all five tools this file invokes resolve the same way, which is a real, independent improvement regardless of whether the PATH-based path was already safe in practice.

points.claim: The new tests assume the existing nested installation: fixture-helpers.cjs symlinked dependencies via a hardcoded 'packages/bitcore-build/node_modules/<name>' path, which would dangle once those dependencies are hoisted.
points.disposition: Fixed, fully agreed. symlinkDependency() now calls the real index.js's own (newly exported) resolvePackageDir() to discover each dependency's actual installed location from bitcore-build's own directory, the same way the production code resolves tools -- correct whether that dependency is nested under bitcore-build (today) or hoisted to a shared root (after Task 2.1). This was a genuine latent bug in the fixture that would have silently broken the very tests meant to protect the post-cutover behavior.

points.claim: The fixtures don't verify the required browser test bundle: only browser:uncompressed (bitcore-lib.js) was exercised, never browser:maketests (tests.js, the actual test bundle Karma/WDIO consume); the Karma check only recorded a config value, and WDIO bundle discovery wasn't tested at all.
points.disposition: Fixed, fully agreed. All three fixtures (hoisted, standalone/nested, space-in-path) now run browser:maketests for real, in addition to browser:uncompressed, and assert the real, on-disk tests.js contains content bundled from the consumer's own test source. A new assertBundleDiscovery() helper then loads the copied karma.conf.js AND wdio.conf.js (the latter's findTestsJs() throws synchronously at module-load time if tests.js doesn't already exist, so this only works once the real bundle has genuinely been generated) with the consumer directory as cwd, and asserts both resolve to that same real, existing tests.js path -- exercising actual bundle discovery, not merely a recorded config value, in every layout including the checkout path containing a space. Building this out surfaced a second, independent pre-existing-design point worth recording: unlike the tool binaries, browserify's -t brfs transform for browser:maketests has always resolved relative to the *consumer's* own cwd (by the plan's own design directive to keep transforms consumer-relative), not to bitcore-build's location -- which is why every real consumer of this pipeline (bitcore-lib, bitcore-lib-cash/-doge/-ltc, bitcore-mnemonic, all three P2P packages) already declares brfs as its own direct dependency rather than relying on bitcore-build to provide it. The standalone/nested fixture was adjusted to model that correctly (brfs reachable from the consumer's own node_modules, not nested under bitcore-build's), rather than changing production behavior that was never part of this bug.

points.claim: Browser acceptance is incomplete, not optional: results.json described real headless-browser execution as 'optional,' but Task 1.1 explicitly requires it; the documented infrastructure failure explains the blockage but does not satisfy the gate.
points.disposition: Fixed, fully agreed -- this was a wording error on my part, not a considered position. The word 'optional' has been removed throughout. The top-level status and acceptanceChecklist now say plainly that this item is UNVERIFIED/incomplete and that Task 1.1 is not being declared fully closed on this environment until real headless execution is re-run successfully, consistent with the plan's own rule that 'missing infrastructure leaves its gate unverified' rather than satisfied or waived.

reviewerFeedbackRound2.source: External agentic reviewer's second pass, after reviewerFeedback's fixes were applied. Reran the focused tests and confirmed 3/3 pass before raising these points.
reviewerFeedbackRound2.verdict: Two of four points were valid and are fixed. The third (browser suites still unverified) restates an already-acknowledged, still-open item and required no further change. The fourth corrects an imprecise closing statement of mine, and is accepted as written.

points.claim: The space-containing fixture still uses a stub Browserify that writes a predetermined marker; it does not produce real bundled content as claimed. Use real Browserify for that fixture.
points.disposition: Fixed, fully agreed. buildSpacedRealFixture() (replacing buildSpacedStubFixture()) now recursively copies bitcore-build's actual installed browserify package into the space-containing fixture root (a real copy, not a symlink -- a symlink would realpath to its real, space-free location and not exercise the space concern at all), while reusing every other real dependency (browserify's own ~44 external dependencies, karma, @wdio/cli, nyc, mocha, brfs, gulp) by symlink for efficiency. Manually verified outside the test run that the resulting bitcore-lib.js begins with browserify's actual UMD bundle-loader wrapper ('require=(function(){function r(e,n,t){...'), not just the marker string, confirming genuine bundling. The prior wording claiming 'real bundled content' for this fixture was inaccurate at the time; it is accurate now.

points.claim: The required real browser suites remain unverified; the corrected status accurately acknowledges this, but Task 1.1 cannot receive an unconditional PASSES yet.
points.disposition: Agreed; already the stated position, unchanged. The top-level status, acceptanceChecklist, and notCompleted fields already say this plainly (added in response to reviewerFeedback's fourth point) and continue to say so: this item is open and required, not satisfied, and Task 1.1 is not being declared unconditionally complete.

points.claim: The PATH refutation tests a different layout: npm adds ancestor .bin directories, which explains the existing repository's success. It does not expose tools nested beneath consumer/node_modules/@bitpay-labs/bitcore-build/node_modules/.bin. The ownership-based fix addresses that original concern.
points.disposition: Agreed, and this sharpens why the fix matters more precisely than my own reviewerFeedback write-up did. My empirical PATH test placed a tool at the true filesystem root, which ancestor-directory PATH climbing from a nested package does reach -- correctly explaining why the ORIGINAL, pre-this-task code happened to work (test:node's bare 'nyc mocha' was, in practice, always resolving root's own devDependency copies via that ancestor climbing, since nyc/mocha were never declared by bitcore-build at all before this task). But bitcore-build's own node_modules is reached from a consumer like bitcore-lib only through the @bitpay-labs symlink -- packages/bitcore-build is bitcore-lib's SIBLING under packages/, not its ancestor -- so a tool nested inside bitcore-build's own node_modules (which is exactly where this task's earlier change caused nyc/mocha to be newly installed, once declared as bitcore-build's own dependencies) is never reached by ancestor PATH climbing at all. Before the resolveBin('nyc')/resolveBin('mocha') fix, this meant the newly-declared, package-owned nyc/mocha were silently never the ones actually invoked -- the bare command name kept resolving to root's unrelated copies instead, coincidentally still working but not for the reason the declaration implied. resolveBin() closes exactly this gap, deterministically invoking the package's own declared tool regardless of what an ancestor directory happens to also provide. My prior refutation is corrected on this point: the PATH-climbing finding explains a real, pre-existing, coincidental success path, but does not show the reviewer's original nested-tool concern was unfounded -- it was well-founded, and is why the fix (already applied) is necessary rather than merely defensive.

points.claim: The working tree is still dirty, contrary to the response's opening claim. No repository files changed during this review.
points.disposition: Agreed on both halves. 'Clean working tree' was imprecise wording on my part immediately after displaying a `git status --short` output that plainly listed several modified/deleted/untracked files -- it was meant to convey 'no stray changes beyond this task's own intended set,' but that is not what 'clean' means in git terminology, and it was confusing at best placed directly under that output. The working tree correctly holds this task's own uncommitted changes throughout (the same M/D/?? set, re-verified via `git status --short` after this round's fixture-helpers.cjs/tool-resolution.test.cjs changes and log regeneration); nothing else changed, and the reviewer's own read-only pass made no repository changes either, which was the substantive point worth confirming.

reviewerFeedbackRound3.source: External agentic reviewer's third pass, after reviewerFeedbackRound2's fixes were applied. Independently reran the focused tests and confirmed 3/3 pass before raising this point; agreed the PATH explanation was resolved and no further wording correction was needed.
reviewerFeedbackRound3.verdict: The one substantive point raised was valid and is fixed. The already-open browser-execution gate is unchanged and remains correctly recorded as incomplete.

points.claim: The round-2 replacement fixture (buildSpacedRealFixture) reintroduces the hardcoded dependency-layout problem: it derives realNodeModules from path.join(BITCORE_BUILD_DIR, 'node_modules'), enumerates that directory, and copies browserify directly from it. After workspace hoisting, browserify can live at the repository root instead, and this fixture would fail with ENOENT even though production resolution works correctly.
points.disposition: Fixed, fully agreed -- this was a real regression to the exact class of bug reviewerFeedback's second point had already found and fixed in symlinkDependency(). Implementing buildSpacedRealFixture from scratch in round 2, I wrote new path-construction code instead of routing it through the already-fixed, layout-agnostic helper, and reintroduced the same mistake. Fixed properly this time: browserify's own real location is now found via resolvePackageDir('browserify', BITCORE_BUILD_DIR) (the same production-derived helper used everywhere else), and -- since a real, unmodified browserify also needs its own transitive dependencies (not just its direct ones) to actually run -- a new linkDependencyClosure() walks browserify's entire real dependency graph recursively, resolving each package from the real location of whichever package actually declares it (resolveInstalledDependencyDir()), not from any single assumed directory. Verified this is not merely a first-level fix: running the real test surfaced two further real bugs the naive one-level-deep version had (a transitive dependency, process-nextick-args, needed by browserify's own nested readable-stream copy; and several of browserify's dependencies -- assert, buffer, events, process, punycode, string_decoder, url, util -- deliberately share a name with a Node core module, which a bare require.resolve() always resolves to the core module for, causing 'could not locate the package root' failures even though the real npm packages are genuinely installed and genuinely needed by browserify's own internal bundling-shim logic). Both are fixed: the closure walk is recursive (not one level), and dependency resolution tries the '/package.json' subpath first (unambiguous even for a core-colliding name) before falling back to production's exports-map-safe walk, exactly mirroring why resolveBin() itself had to stop using a bare '/package.json' subpath for @wdio/cli. Re-verified 3/3 tests pass, stable across three repeated runs, and manually confirmed (outside the test run) that the resulting bundle still begins with browserify's real UMD wrapper.

points.claim: Real headless-browser execution is required and still unverified, correctly recorded in results.json.
points.disposition: Agreed; no change made or needed. This remains the one open, required acceptance item -- see acceptanceChecklist and notCompleted, unchanged since reviewerFeedback's fourth point.

greenEvidence.note: Replaces the removed hoisted-layout.test.cjs (see redEvidence.note). Reuses the same fixture concept -- a byte-for-byte copy of today's real index.js/karma.conf.js/wdio.conf.js inside a disposable temp directory, never a symlink to the real repository -- now asserting success instead of the old failure, plus the additional layouts/concerns the GREEN acceptance criteria call for. Updated after reviewerFeedback to also exercise browser:maketests and real Karma/WDIO bundle discovery, and to discover fixture dependency locations via the real resolvePackageDir() instead of a hardcoded nesting assumption.
greenEvidence.command: node --test test/*.test.cjs (run from packages/bitcore-build; also invoked as `npm test` there)

tests.name: under a hoisted (npm workspaces) layout, the helper resolves tools from its own location, produces real bundles, and Karma/WDIO discover them
tests.covers: Task's core fix. Fixture root mirrors npm workspaces' hoisted install: real browserify/karma/@wdio-cli/nyc/mocha/brfs (symlinked via resolvePackageDir() from bitcore-build's own already-installed copies, not stubs) and the copied helper live at the fixture root; the consumer package directory has zero node_modules of its own. Asserts (a) neither of the helper's old hardcoded per-consumer .bin paths nor the old default karma.conf.js lookup path exists under this layout, (b) the captured browser:uncompressed AND browser:maketests commands each embed browserify's real, resolved absolute bin path (not the old fixed-depth guesses), (c) actually running both tasks succeeds and writes real bundles (bitcore-lib.js and tests.js) to the consumer directory containing content bundled from the consumer's own source, and (d) the copied karma.conf.js and wdio.conf.js both genuinely discover that real, on-disk tests.js from the consumer's own cwd.

tests.name: the helper also resolves tools, bundles, and bundle discovery when tools are nested per-consumer (a plain, non-workspaces npm install), protecting external users of bitcore-build
tests.covers: GREEN acceptance's 'nested standalone installation fixture'. Tool packages are nested directly under the copied helper's own node_modules (a plain npm install's non-hoisted layout, e.g. for an external consumer never adopting workspaces); brfs is instead reachable from the consumer's own node_modules, matching how every real consumer of this pipeline in this repository already declares it directly (see reviewerFeedback). The same real-bundling and bundle-discovery assertions as the hoisted test pass.

tests.name: tool invocation, bundling, and bundle discovery survive a checkout path containing a space
tests.covers: GREEN acceptance's 'checkout path containing spaces'. The fixture root's own path deliberately contains a space; a REAL browserify is recursively copied (not symlinked -- a symlink's target realpaths to its actual, space-free location in the repository checkout, which would defeat the point of this fixture) into that space-containing tree. Its entire real dependency closure (not just its direct dependencies) is discovered and symlinked in by recursively walking each dependency's own real package.json from wherever it actually resolves (linkDependencyClosure()/resolveInstalledDependencyDir()) -- layout-agnostic, not assumed to live under bitcore-build's own node_modules. Asserts both the browser:uncompressed and browser:maketests constructed commands double-quote that genuinely space-containing resolved bin path, that both invocations run REAL browserify successfully and write real bundled content (confirmed to contain browserify's own UMD bundle wrapper, not merely a marker string) to the consumer directory, and that karma.conf.js/wdio.conf.js still correctly discover the resulting real tests.js. (Two earlier revisions are superseded: a stub browserify that only wrote a predetermined marker, then a real-copy version that hardcoded path.join(BITCORE_BUILD_DIR, 'node_modules') for the rest of the tree and only resolved browserify's direct dependencies one level deep; see reviewerFeedbackRound2 and reviewerFeedbackRound3.)

greenEvidence.debuggingNoteWorthPreserving: The first implementation attempt resolved tools via require.resolve(packageName + '/package.json', {paths:[__dirname]}), matching how bitcore-lib's own require.resolve('@bitpay-labs/bitcore-build') check already worked. Running it for real against the actual installed @wdio/cli immediately failed with ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED: @wdio/cli declares a strict package.json "exports" map with no './package.json' subpath, which Node's exports enforcement rejects regardless of the file's real on-disk existence. This was caught only by exercising real tool packages (browserify/karma/@wdio-cli symlinked into the fixture from bitcore-build's actual installed copies) rather than hand-rolled stubs, and only by then running the real consumer regression suites end-to-end (see consumerRegressionEvidence) -- both a synthetic-only fixture using stub manifests and skipping the real-suite run would have missed this. Fixed by resolving through the package's normal require.resolve(packageName) entry point (always subject to the exports map's own declared conditions, which do allow requiring the package itself) and then walking up directories to find that package's own package.json by name (resolvePackageDir()), rather than importing '/package.json' as a subpath.

consumerRegressionEvidence.method: Ran the real root test:<package> aliases (`cd packages/<x> && npm run test`, i.e. `gulp test`) against the actual Lerna-bootstrapped installation -- each consumer's node_modules/@bitpay-labs/bitcore-build is a real Lerna symlink to the one edited packages/bitcore-build directory, so this exercises the production fix directly, not a copy.
